question: A 61-year-old man comes to the physician because of several episodes of dark urine over the past 2 weeks. He does not have dysuria or flank pain. He works in a factory that produces dyes. Since an accident at work 5 years ago, he has had moderate hearing loss bilaterally. He takes no medications. He has smoked a pack of cigarettes daily for 29 years and drinks one alcoholic beverage daily. Vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. His urine is pink; urinalysis shows 80 RBC/hpf but no WBCs. Cystoscopy shows a 3-cm mass in the bladder mucosa. The mass is resected. Pathologic examination shows an urothelial carcinoma with penetration into the muscular layer. An x-ray of the chest and a CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis with contrast show a normal upper urinary tract and normal lymph nodes. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.opa: Transurethral resection of tumor with intravesical chemotherapy
options.opc: Transurethral resection of tumor with intravesical BCG instillation

CHAIN: "Cystoscopy reveals a mass" -> "Pathology confirms urothelial carcinoma" -> "Tumor has muscular invasion" -> "Guidelines recommend radical cystectomy for muscle-invasive bladder cancer" -> 80%

CHAIN: "Patient's tumor is muscle-invasive" -> "Standard management includes radical cystectomy" -> "Other options like BCG are for non-muscle invasive" -> "Radical cystectomy is the most appropriate next step" -> 88%
enhanced_information: The patient has been diagnosed with muscle-invasive urothelial carcinoma, as indicated by the tumor's penetration into the muscular layer of the bladder. Standard management for muscle-invasive bladder cancer is radical cystectomy, which is supported by multiple guidelines. The reasoning chains consistently point to radical cystectomy as the most appropriate next step, with a high level of consensus (85-90%). Other options, such as intravesical BCG therapy, are reserved for non-muscle invasive disease and are not appropriate in this case. The retrieved evidence path regarding BCG does not apply here, as it pertains to a different treatment context. Therefore, the most appropriate next step in management is radical cystectomy.
